content_of_post_to_comment: One of my favorite accidents in history is the time the historical Buddha was accidentally venerated as a Christian saint for almost a thousand years. Basically what happened was that a fourth century Mahayana Buddhist text made its way to West Asia, and when translated into Arabic in the 8th century, the Sanskrit word Bodhisattva (a would be Buddha who delayed enlightenment to continue to incarnate and aid others) morphed into Budhasaf. The text migrated further west, and Budhasaf eventually made its way into the 10th century Georgian epic Balavariani. The story was translated into Greek by a Georgian monk, and Budhasaf became Iosaphat. Then, in 1048, the text was translated from Greek into Latin and Iosaphat became Josaphat. Through myriad translations and iterations, the story morphed into a more Christian centric narrative, inventing a Christian hermit figure named Barlaam who supposedly taught Josaphat, but the major hallmarks of the historical Buddha’s life legend were all still included. (A prince sees the four marks of existence, gives up his throne, and wanders the countryside to find enlightenment/divinity.) The story of Barlaam and Josaphat spread across Europe, eventually becoming so popular that the Church assigned the Buddha a feast day. I wasn’t until the nineteenth century that scholars began to translate Asian religious texts and we realized that Josaphat was a corruption of the term Bodhisattva. Even still, Barlaam and Josaphat weren’t removed from the liturgical calendar until 1960.
comment: The fascinating tension here is that cultural translation didn't just preserve a story—it created a new religious identity. At what point does adaptation become the birth of a different tradition?
